paragraphs.text: The Extraordinary Watkin Tench At the end of the 18th century, life for the average British citizen was changing. The population grew as health improved and industrialisation took hold. Land and resources, however, were limited, and families could not guarantee jobs for all their children. Poor or destitute people had few options, and increasing numbers turned to crime to survive. Britain’s prisons were no longer large enough to hold the growing population of convicted criminals, leaving many towns and governments uncertain about what to do. Another feature of the 18th century was the exploration of other continents. Many ships needed crew members willing to risk months-long voyages across vast oceans, but the work was dangerous and few chose it freely. With so many citizens unemployed or convicted of crimes, however, some had little choice. Watkin Tench was one member of this new lower class. Between 1788 and 1868, approximately 161,700 convicts were transported to the Australian colonies of New South Wales, Van Diemen’s Land and Western Australia. Tench was among those who signed on for a dangerous journey. When his ship departed in 1788, he signed up for three years’ service with the First Fleet.

Apart from his years in Australia, little is known about Tench’s life in Britain. He is said to have been born on 6 October 1758 in Chester, Cheshire, and to have come from a respectable background. He was the son of Fisher Tench, a dancing master who ran a boarding school in the town, and Margaritta Tarleton of the Liverpool Tarletons. He grew up among a more privileged class of British citizens, and his family taught formal dance to wealthy children. Although we do not know exactly how Tench was educated in this small town, his Australian diaries show that he was well educated: they are written in excellent English, a skill not everyone possessed in the 18th century. Beyond this, little is known about his beginnings or how he came to be convicted of a crime. After his voyage began, however, his life changed dramatically.

During the harsh voyage, which lasted many months, Tench described the landscapes of different places. On the journey to Australia, he saw scenes that were new and unfamiliar. When the crew arrived, uncertain about their new lives, they established a British colony. Governor Phillip had complete authority over its inhabitants. Though still a young man, he was enlightened for his time. Accounts of other British colonies had taught him that conflict with the land’s Indigenous peoples often caused strife and hardship, so he personally intended to establish harmonious relations with local Aboriginal people. His task was made more difficult by the composition of his crew. Other colonies had been established by middle-class merchants and craftspeople; his crew were convicts with few skills beyond those associated with their criminal pasts. As well as making peace with Aboriginal people, Phillip had to reform and discipline the colony’s convicts.

From the beginning, Tench stood apart from the other convicts. Early in his time in Australia, he rose quickly through the ranks and received additional authority and responsibility over the convict crew members. Yet he also differed from the upper-class officials who governed them. He treated the workers humanely, regarding them not as common criminals but as trained military men. Under his authority, the chains used to control convicts during the voyage were removed. Tench also showed mercy towards Aboriginal people. Governor Phillip often pursued violent responses to conflict, but Tench strongly disagreed. On one occasion, he could not carry out Phillip’s order to punish ten Aboriginal people.

When he first arrived, Tench was fearful of and contemptuous towards Aboriginal people because the two cultures did not understand one another. Gradually, however, he came to know individuals and became their close friend. He understood that Aboriginal people would not create conflict if peaceful solutions were sought. Although violence continued, Tench’s efforts encouraged more peaceful negotiations between the two groups over territory and land use.

Meanwhile, many changes were made to the new colony. The Hawkesbury River was named by Governor Phillip in June 1789. Many bird species native to the river were hunted by travelling colonists. The colonists were having a great impact on the land and natural resources. Though the colonists had made a lot of progress in the untamed lands of Australia, there were still limits. The convicts were notoriously ill-informed about Australian geography, as was evident in the attempt by twenty absconders to walk from Sydney to China in 1791, believing: “China might be easily reached, being not more than a hundred miles distant, and separated only by a river.” In reality, thousands of miles of ocean separated the two.

Much of Australia remained unexplored by the convicts, and even Tench knew little of what lay beyond the established boundaries of the colony. Slowly but surely, the colonists expanded into the surrounding region. A few days after arriving at their original location, Botany Bay, the fleet moved to the more suitable Port Jackson, where a settlement was established at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788. This second location was strange and unfamiliar, and the fleet remained alert to anything suspicious. Although Tench had befriended Aboriginal people at Botany Bay, he could not be certain that the new area was uninhabited. He recalled his first steps on this unfamiliar ground with a boy who helped guide him. There he met an elderly Aboriginal man.

Questions 1–6
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In Boxes 1–6 on your answer sheet, write

 TRUE                         if the statement agrees with the information

 FALSE                        if the statement contradicts the information

 NOT GIVEN                    if there is no information on this
1 _________________ There was a great deal of information available about the life of Tench before he
arrived in Australia.
2 _________________ Tench drew pictures to illustrate different places during the voyage.
3 _________________ Other military personnel in New South Wales did not treat convicts in the same
way as Tench did.
4 _________________ Tench’s view of Aboriginal people remained unchanged during his time in
Australia.
5 _________________ An Aboriginal person gave Tench gifts of food when they first met.
6 _________________ The convicts had a good knowledge of Australian geography.
